screens.title: Final Examination and Answer Key
screens.subtitle: Prepare, review, and apply core IoT concepts through concise questions and worked solutions.

narration.text: This final chapter collects the key exam items and answers that show what you can do with IoT fundamentals. You will see multiple-choice checks, short-answer explanations, code-analysis exercises, and a full practical design problem for a smart refrigerator. Each item highlights the principle behind a correct answer so you understand not just what is right, but why. Reviewing these questions helps you recognize common mistakes like forgetting a delay in a microcontroller loop, missing a network loop in an MQTT client, or misplacing secrets in source code. As you study, focus on cause-and-effect: what design choices control latency, reliability, and security? The practical problem combines Arduino sensing, serial transfer, Raspberry Pi storage, and cloud uploads — a short, realistic pipeline you can reproduce. By the end of this chapter you should be able to explain IoT layers, compare microcontrollers to single-board computers, justify MQTT for low-power telemetry, and identify simple fixes for recurring code errors. Think about which parts you would implement first if you built a real device, and which parts you would harden for production.

screens.title: Interpreting the multiple-choice answers
screens.subtitle: Why each correct choice is correct and what common distractors mean.

narration.text: Multiple-choice items in this exam test clear distinctions between IoT concepts and common misreads. For example, the primary difference between the traditional internet and the Internet of Things is not speed or whether everything is wireless; it is the connection of physical objects to each other and to cloud services for sensing and action. That distinction matters because it determines the kinds of constraints you must design for: power, physical interfaces, and local control. Similarly, a correct answer identified the edge or gateway layer as the bridge that performs local processing and connects devices to the network. Misreading that as the cloud layer confuses where latency-sensitive logic should run. The exam also checks simple factual knowledge: the Arduino loop function runs continuously after setup, and Serial. begin initializes serial communication at a given baud rate; these are small facts that matter when you debug behavior. Practice by turning each question into a one-sentence explanation of the constraint or trade-off it tests. That habit helps you avoid distractors that sound plausible but ignore the system constraint under test. screens.title: Five layers of IoT architecture
screens.subtitle: Device, edge/gateway, network, cloud, and application — roles and why they matter.

narration.text: The five-layer model in the exam provides a useful checklist when designing IoT systems. The device layer is where sensors and actuators interact with the physical world; examples include analog temperature inputs and digital door switches. The edge or gateway layer collects device data and can run local processing — for instance, threshold logic that must act immediately or data filtering to reduce bandwidth. The network layer provides the transport: Wi‑Fi, cellular, or low-power WANs that determine latency and reach. The cloud layer stores, processes, and analyzes data at scale; use it for long-term trend analysis, heavy computation, or centralized dashboards. Finally, the application layer presents data and controls to users via mobile apps or web dashboards. Crucially, deciding which layer performs time-critical actions is a design decision: hybrid architectures move quick decisions to the edge or device and delegate heavy analytics to the cloud. Misplacing responsibilities can increase latency or waste power, so always evaluate where latency, reliability, and privacy constraints are strictest before assigning a task to a layer. Five layers of IoT architecture means place low-latency, private, or bandwidth-sensitive processing on the device or edge; reserve long-term storage and heavy analysis for the cloud.. screens.title: Arduino sketch: loop, Serial.begin, and sampling rates
screens.subtitle: Read the sketch, spot the issue, and apply the fix.

narration.text: We analyze a short Arduino sketch that reads an analog sensor and prints values continuously. The sketch initializes serial at 9600 baud and repeatedly runs analogRead inside the continuous loop. The underlying issue is absence of any delay or sampling control. Without a delay, the loop executes as fast as possible, which floods the serial link and the monitor, making the output hard to interpret and possibly overloading downstream readers. A practical fix is to add a delay of an appropriate length — for example, one second — or to implement a timed sampling pattern using the board clock. Adding a controlled sampling rate stabilizes the data stream and reduces power and C P U usage. A related point: Serial. begin sets the serial baud and must be called in setup to initialize communication. A common misconception is to think faster sampling is always better; in many sensor applications, sampling more frequently than the sensor bandwidth or application needs wastes energy and yields noisy data. A reflective question: what sampling rate would you choose for a temperature sensor that changes slowly, and why?

keyIdea.title: Fix: control sampling rate
keyIdea.text: Add an appropriate delay or timed sampling to prevent flooding serial output and to match sampling to sensor behavior.

content.html:

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
}
void loop() {
  int val = analogRead(A0);
  Serial.println(val);

Suggested fix
Add delay(1000); to loop or use millis-based timing to sample at a controlled rate.
Key Takeaway

screens.title: Why MQTT is preferred for frequent, small updates
screens.subtitle: Lightweight messaging, persistent connections, and QoS suited to constrained devices.

narration.text: MQTT appears in the exam as the preferred protocol for frequent, small sensor updates from battery-powered devices. The reasons in this chapter are practical: MQTT is a lightweight publish–subscribe protocol that maintains a persistent connection, reducing the setup overhead of repeated HTTP requests. That means devices avoid repeated TCP and TLS handshakes, saving energy. MQTT also supports Quality of Service levels that allow you to balance delivery guarantees against resource use. A common exam distractor is HTTP with polling: while simple, polling requires frequent request setup and response handling, which consumes more bandwidth and power. A misconception to watch for is assuming MQTT guarantees delivery without configuration: QoS settings determine behavior and must be chosen based on acceptable trade-offs. For example, QoS 0 is fire-and-forget and uses the fewest resources, appropriate for frequent telemetry where occasional loss is acceptable. Always match protocol choices to device constraints, power budget, and reliability requirements. screens.title: Why use SQLite for Raspberry Pi data logging
screens.subtitle: Lightweight, serverless SQL for local persistence on single-board computers.

narration.text: SQLite is recommended in the exam as an effective choice for Raspberry Pi data logging because it is lightweight, serverless, and supports S Q L querying without requiring a separate database server process. For many IoT prototypes a Raspberry Pi acts as a local aggregator and needs a simple way to persist readings; SQLite provides transactional storage without the complexity of managing a dedicated database service. That means backups, queries, and simple indexing are straightforward, reducing development friction. A common contrast is with time-series databases that are optimized for high-volume temporal data; those may be appropriate for large deployments but add operational overhead. In small to medium projects, SQLite offers a pragmatic balance between capability and simplicity. When you design your data schema, include timestamps and a sent flag for cloud uploads to track which rows have been uploaded. This pattern supports reliable uploads and retry logic on intermittent networks. screens.title: Secrets, transport, and simple security measures
screens.subtitle: Environment variables, TLS, authentication, firmware signing, and network segmentation.

narration.text: Security questions in the exam focus on practical, small-step defenses you can add without redesigning the system. First, store A P I keys and other secrets in environment variables or secure hardware stores rather than hardcoding them in source control; this prevents accidental disclosure when code is shared. Second, always encrypt data in transit using TLS or HTTPS; unencrypted HTTP allows an attacker to intercept and read data. Third, use strong authentication: A P I keys, certificates, or tokens ensure only authorized devices can send data. The practical problem also mentions signed firmware updates — this prevents attackers from pushing malicious images. Finally, network-level controls like firewalls and segmentation reduce exposure of devices on a local network. A common misconception is that small prototypes do not need these measures; in reality, even simple devices can leak data or be co-opted into larger attacks. Prioritize easy wins first: move secrets out of code and enable encrypted transport. Secrets, transport, and simple security measures means keep secrets out of code, encrypt transport, authenticate devices, and add firmware signing and network segmentation as practical next steps.. screens.title: ThingSpeak update bug and rate limits in Python
screens.subtitle: Identify and fix timing errors that violate cloud API limits.

narration.text: The Python snippet that tries to update ThingSpeak every 15 seconds contains a clear bug: it sleeps for one second between requests. That violates the platform rate limit and will cause the service to reject repeated calls. The fix is straightforward: increase the sleep interval to match the required 15 seconds or implement a timer that enforces the minimum time between updates. Also, avoid hardcoding A P I keys in the script; use environment variables and fail gracefully if the key is missing. In production you might batch or throttle updates and check response status codes to confirm successful writes. A misconception is assuming the service will silently queue requests; many services return explicit error codes or zero responses when updates are too fast. Error handling and backoff logic should be added so your client respects the remote service limits and retries responsibly. ThingSpeak update bug and rate limits in Python means match your request cadence to the cloud platform's rate limits and add error handling for rejected requests.. In practical terms, identify and fix timing errors that violate cloud api limits.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › ThingSpeak Bug
Original code excerpt
import requests
import time

API_KEY = "YOUR_KEY"
URL = "https://api.thingspeak.com/update"

while True:
    temp = 25.5
    response = requests.get(URL, params={"api_key": API_KEY, "field1": temp})
    print(response.status_code)
    time.sleep(1)
The sleep value should be changed to 15 seconds to comply with the ThingSpeak rate limit and avoid rejected writes.
Fix
Replace time.sleep(1) with time.sleep(15) and move API keys to environment variables to prevent accidental exposure.
Pro tip

Check response codes and apply exponential backoff on errors rather than aggressive retries.

Key Takeaway

Obey API rate limits and handle error responses to maintain reliable uploads.

screens.title: MQTT client must run a network loop
screens.subtitle: Why starting the network loop is required to receive messages.

narration.text: The MQTT subscriber snippet connects and subscribes but never starts the network loop, so incoming messages are never processed. MQTT clients must run a loop that processes network events and dispatches callbacks. In many client libraries the loop is started with a blocking call that keeps the client alive, or a non-blocking start that runs in a background thread. Without that loop, the client does not read from the socket and on_message handlers will not run. A common beginner mistake is to call connect and subscribe and then expect callbacks without the loop. The practical fix in the exam answer is to add a call such as starting the client loop forever or starting a background loop. This is an important difference between establishing a session and actually processing messages. When designing systems, remember to pair network setup with an appropriate event loop or thread so the subscription behaves as intended. MQTT client must run a network loop means start the mqtt client loop to process incoming network data and trigger on_message callbacks.. In practical terms, why starting the network loop is required to receive messages.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Run the loop

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › MQTT Subscriber
Problem snippet
import paho.mqtt.client as mqtt

def on_message(client, userdata, msg):
    print(msg.payload)

client = mqtt.Client()
client.on_message = on_message
client.connect("localhost", 1883)
client.subscribe("sensors/temperature")
# missing: client.loop_forever() or client.loop_start()
Add a network loop call, such as loop_forever, to process messages continuously.
Fix
Append client.loop_forever() for a blocking loop, or client.loop_start() to run in the background.
Key Takeaway

Connection is not processing. Start the network loop to receive messages.

screens.title: Smart refrigerator system design
screens.subtitle: End-to-end requirements and component responsibilities for the capstone problem.

narration.text: The practical problem asks you to design a smart refrigerator that monitors temperature and door status with concrete timing and alert requirements. The design divides responsibilities between an Arduino and a Raspberry Pi. The Arduino reads the analog temperature sensor and the digital door switch every five seconds and manages the buzzer when the door remains open for more than thirty seconds. It serializes readings into compact JSON for transfer: a pattern that keeps messages simple and parseable. The Raspberry Pi receives serial messages, stores them in SQLite with timestamps, and uploads aggregated data to the cloud every two minutes. Additionally, it runs simple alert logic: if temperature stays above eight degrees Celsius for five minutes, it sends an email alert. Finally, the Pi runs a lightweight Flask dashboard to display the current temperature and door status. This split keeps time-critical control on the Arduino and heavier tasks like storage, aggregation, and cloud communication on the Pi, illustrating the device/edge/cloud pattern from earlier lessons. Smart refrigerator system design means keep immediate control and safety logic on the device; delegate storage, aggregation, and external notifications to the single-board computer and cloud.. In practical terms, end-to-end requirements and component responsibilities for the capstone problem.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Arduino and Raspberry Pi example code walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Walk through the provided Arduino sketch and Pi Python service for the smart refrigerator.

narration.text: The chapter includes example code for the Arduino and the Raspberry Pi that together implement the smart refrigerator pipeline. On the Arduino, readings are converted from analog values into Celsius and packed into a small JSON object. The code uses an internal pull-up for the door switch and tracks how long the door is open using millis to trigger the buzzer after thirty seconds. It writes the serialized JSON to Serial and delays for five seconds between samples. On the Raspberry Pi side, a simple Python service opens the serial port, writes to SQLite, and batches uploads to ThingSpeak every two minutes. It maintains an alert start timestamp so that a temperature exceeding the threshold for longer than five minutes triggers a webhook. The Pi also hosts a Flask route that reads the latest row from SQLite and presents the current temperature and door status. Together, these examples show common patterns: JSON over serial, a sent flag for uploads, and simple temporal logic for alerts. A useful exercise is to simulate intermittent network failures and observe that the Pi's local store preserves readings until uploads succeed.

narration.text: These three compact concept cards summarize the chapter. First, remember the five-layer IoT architecture: device, edge, network, cloud, and application — and place latency-sensitive logic at the device or edge. Second, prefer lightweight protocols such as MQTT for frequent, small updates from battery-powered devices, and configure QoS to match your reliability needs. Third, follow practical security habits: keep A P I keys out of source, use TLS for transport, and add simple protections like signed firmware and network segmentation. Together these concepts guide reliable prototype design and help you avoid common exam pitfalls. Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Final Reminders
Design by constraints
Place low-latency logic near the sensors; use cloud for heavy analysis.
Protocol efficiency
Prefer MQTT for frequent, small telemetry and configure QoS thoughtfully.
Practical security
Keep secrets out of source, enable encryption, and add simple firmware and network protections.
Final takeaway

Use the exam answers as templates for reasoned decision-making in real projects: explain the why, not just the what.
